cues.text: A Farm Boy Drawn to the Priesthood

Born in 1803 near Cuet, in the Ain region of France, Peter Chanel was educated by a devoted parish priest, Fr. Jean-Marie Trompier, who instilled in him from boyhood a desire for both the priesthood and foreign missionary work.

Ordained a diocesan priest in 1827, Peter spent his early years teaching in a seminary before joining the newly founded Society of Mary (Marists) in 1831, hoping the order would open a path to the missions he had long desired.
Sent to Oceania
In 1836, the priests' branch of the Marists received formal papal approval and was assigned responsibility for new missionary territory in the little-known southwest Pacific.
Peter was named superior of the first band of seven Marist missionaries, who set sail from Le Havre on Christmas Eve under the leadership of Bishop Jean-Baptiste Pompallier.
Alone on Futuna
In November 1837, Pompallier left Peter and a lay brother on the remote island of Futuna , promising to return within six months — a promise not fulfilled for nearly five years.

Peter labored virtually alone, mastering an unfamiliar language, adapting to life among warring island tribes and visiting whalers and traders, and enduring severe material want, all while maintaining, by contemporary accounts, remarkable patience and gentleness despite very limited visible success.
Martyrdom

Peter's quiet, patient ministry began at last to bear fruit, and when the son of the island's chief, Niuliki, asked to be baptized, the chief's jealousy and anger at the new religion's growing influence reached a breaking point.
At his instigation, a band of men attacked Peter, who was killed without offering resistance or complaint on 28 April 1841.
A Slow Path to Recognition
Because reliable eyewitness testimony was difficult to establish, the Church took decades to be satisfied that Peter had died specifically out of hatred for the Catholic faith.
His formal recognition as a martyr was delayed; he was beatified only in 1889.
In the years following his death, however, most of the island, including members of the chief's family, eventually converted to Catholicism.
Legacy
Canonized in 1954 by Pope Pius XII, Peter Chanel is remembered as the protomartyr of Oceania — the first martyr of the entire South Pacific mission field.
His relics were returned to Futuna at the islanders' own request in 1977 and rest today in a basilica built at his place of martyrdom.
After his death, a modest missionary's quiet, largely unrewarded labor became the seed of a lasting Catholic presence across the islands he served.
